blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define internal and external growth, explain what pushes a firm to grow and how the growth is financed, and trace what internal growth does to the firm and its workers.

blocks.heading: Two ways to grow
blocks.text: A firm grows internally when it expands through its own resources - opening a second branch, installing another production line, taking on more workers - and the firm remains itself throughout. It grows externally when it combines with another firm: a merger joins two firms into one by agreement, and a takeover sees one firm buy control of another. The two paths differ in what they need: internal growth needs time and finance; external growth needs a willing partner or the money to buy one.

blocks.heading: Why firms grow, and how it is paid for
blocks.text: The push to grow comes from the firm's aims: higher profit, a larger share of the market, and the lower average costs that growing output tends to bring. Growth needs paying for before it pays back - a second line must be built before it fills a single bottle - so the firm draws on retained profit, borrows, or asks its owners to invest more. The effects then spread through the firm: output and revenue rise together, and the workforce grows, giving workers more openings and clearer promotion paths. The strain spreads too: managers who ran one line now run two, and the personal contact a small workforce allowed is harder to keep as the payroll lengthens.

blocks.heading: Kaoko Juice builds a second line
blocks.text: Kaoko Juice in Opuwo sold 240 000 litres of juice in 2024. In 2025 it opened a second bottling line, funded from retained profit and a bank loan, and by 2026 sales had reached 500 000 litres a year. No other firm joined it, so the growth was internal: the same firm, with more of its own equipment and 30 more workers. The 30 extra jobs are the gain workers feel directly; the loan repayments are the cost the firm carries until the extra output earns them back. A family brewery in Bavaria tells the same story on another continent - new vats bought from its own profits, more beer, more brewers - because internal growth keeps every step in the owner's hands.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Whether a bigger output makes each unit cheaper is the question 3.5.5 takes up next, and what firms do with the workers they hire is traced in topic 3.6.
